content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a guideline on school health services, which is available in both electronic and print formats. The electronic version has the ISBN 978-92-4-002939-2, while the print version is identified by ISBN 978-92-4-002940-8. WHO is not liable for any damages arising from the use of the material. The guideline emphasizes the critical role of schools in fostering the health and well-being of children and adolescents. Schools provide a platform for young people to acquire knowledge, socioemotional skills, self-regulation, resilience, and critical thinking abilities, all of which contribute to a healthy future. Access to education and supportive school environments is strongly linked to improved health outcomes, reduced dropout rates, and enhanced educational attainment, performance, employment, and productivity. WHO has long recognized the connection between health and education and the potential for schools to safeguard student health and well-being. In 1995, WHO launched the Global School Health Initiative to strengthen health promotion in schools. Among the strategies, linking children with health services is particularly significant. Early detection of health conditions can lead to better management or prevention. Schools and school health services offer opportunities for timely interventions for various conditions, including anxiety, depression, behavioral disorders, diabetes, obesity, and undernutrition. School health services are uniquely positioned to address the health needs of school-age children for several reasons. First, they operate where most children are present and have access to families. Second, they are free at the point of use, overcoming barriers such as transportation issues, limited community services, and inconvenient locations or appointment systems. This makes them particularly effective in serving underprivileged populations. Third, they positively impact multiple determinants of health and are highly valued by students, parents, and communities. Despite these advantages, school health services have historically been overlooked and under-researched. This WHO guideline aims to address this gap by strongly recommending the implementation of comprehensive school health services. The guideline comes at a critical time, as the COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the essential link between health and education. The pandemic has exacerbated existing issues, such as anxiety, depression, mental distress, disrupted physical activity, increased child maltreatment, and exposure to risks in the digital environment. The guideline seeks to create a common language around school health services, promote evidence-based care through a menu of interventions, and strengthen school nursing and health professions globally. If implemented effectively, school health services can provide a safety net for children and yield lasting benefits for their health and well-being. WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom emphasizes the importance of adequately resourced and well-implemented school health services in improving the health of children worldwide.
